title: The Executor Accord separates a Prime Agent's strategy from its operations, with the Executor supplying operational insurance
content:
A.2.2.6.1 calls the Executor Accord Primitive "the foundational mechanism that allows Prime Agents to operate autonomously according to the strategy specified in their Agent Artifacts with automated operational insurance provided by separate Operational Executor Agents that delegate the work to GovOps actors."

Three separations are packed into that sentence. The **Prime** owns strategy, expressed as documents in its Artifact. A **separate Operational Executor Agent** owns execution and carries the operational risk — the Atlas calls this "insurance," meaning the Prime's autonomy is underwritten by someone else's operational accountability. **GovOps actors** do the actual work, delegated one further step down.

The Accord itself is genuinely bilateral rather than imposed: A.2.2.6.1.1.1.1 requires the Prime and the Executor to reach consensus and enter the details into Powerhouse "along with independent confirmation from each Agent that they agree to those terms," and A.2.2.6.1.2.3 makes that dual confirmation a validity requirement. Core GovOps' only substantive check is that the terms are "reasonably specific" (A.2.2.6.1.1.1.2) — it does not judge whether they are good.

Why this is load-bearing: it is what lets a Prime Agent be a thin strategic entity. A Prime never needs its own operations team, because operational capability is a market it buys into by Accord. It also explains why the Accord is non-deactivatable — without a counterparty, a Prime has no hands.
description: Primes hold the strategy in their Artifact; separate Operational Executor Agents run it via delegated GovOps actors, and both sides must independently confirm the Accord terms.
